title: Lacson alleges House push to remove 'Anti-Epal' clause from 2027 budget
summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Wednesday floated that certain members of the House of Representatives are seeking to have the provision barring politicians from the distribution of financial assistance…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 12:02am

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Wednesday floated that certain members of the House of Representatives are seeking to have the provision barring politicians from the distribution of financial assistance removed from the 2027 national budget.

This was raised amid the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P253.34 billion budget of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) and its attached agencies for the next fiscal year.
During the session, Lacson asked budget sponsor Senator Risa Hontiveros if the DSWD has full control over the disbursement of the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS).
Hontiveros, who was taking answers from DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian, said the agency is maintaining that it has full control over the decision-making in the AICS program.
“I’m sorry, but I don’t believe that. That's why some congressmen are pushing for the AICS,” Lacson said.
“Actually, meron tayong parang I think forthcoming na bicam. Ito ‘yung sa Bawal Epal, gusto nila tanggalin ‘yung provision eh, sa Bawal Epal. They want to retain that, na merong epal,” he added.

(Actually, I believe there’s a bicameral conference coming up. This is regarding the Anti-Epal provision. They want to remove that provision. They want to retain that there is indeed an epal among them.)

The word “epal” is Filipino slang for someone who wants attention or wants to be noticed, especially in a way that’s inappropriate or self-serving. In politics, it usually refers to officials who take credit for government projects to boost their public image or electoral appeal.
In the 2026 General Appropriations Act (GAA), a so-called "anti-epal" special provision was included, preventing politicians from using government programs, projects, or funds to promote themselves.
Guarantee letters

During the budget deliberations, Lacson likewise questioned a provision in the House version of the 2027 budget bill which he said would allow the settlement of unpaid claims from guarantee letters issued in 2024.
He pointed out that the P34.269 billion allocation for the AICS program under the 2024 GAA had already been fully obligated.
“Ang sinasabi po rito, ‘yung guarantee letters issued in 2024, babayaran sa GAA in 2027. Parang nag-issue ng tseke na walang pondo ng 2024. Popondohan ng GAA ng 2027,” Lacson said.

(It seems that guarantee letters issued in 2024 will be paid for through the GAA in 2027. It’s like saying checks were issued in 2024 without any funds to back them. The 2027 GAA will be the one to pay for it.)

Lacson was referring to Special Provision No. 2 in the House General Appropriations Bill (HGAB), where the DSWD’s proposed budget provides for a “Protective Services Program for Individuals and Families in Difficult Circumstances.”

Under the special provision, the amount appropriated for such “shall likewise be used for the payment of arrears to accredited and/or partner service providers arising from the issuance of guarantee letter in fiscal year 2024, subject to the availability of funds and compliance with applicable budgeting, accounting, and auditing laws, rules and regulations.”
Hontiveros admitted that such information was shocking, but said there were service providers that belatedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents.
“Kaya ngayon lamang ni-request and special provision na ito sa fiscal year 2027,” she said.
(That’s why this special provision is being requested only now for fiscal year 2027.) —LDF, GMA News
